newsitem.title: UK: State may be asked to fund UK's new tilting trains.
newsitem.headline: State may be asked to fund UK's new tilting trains.

text.p: Britain's rail industry would have to seek funding from the government if private bidders cannot produce cost-effective plans to make future passenger train services cheaper with new tilting trains than using slower, conventional rolling stock, officials said on Tuesday.

"In the event that there will be a premium price required, then we will have to consult with the government," Roger Salmon director general of the Office of Passenger Rail Franchising (OPRAF) told a news conference. Earlier OPRAF and Railtrack Plc had unveiled a 1.5 billion stg plan to upgrade a busy UK trunk route for tilting trains alongside its privatisation.

OPRAF has decided to require all parties interested in seeking the operating franchise for the Inter City West Coast company to submit two parallel bids -- one based on a business plan with conventional trains and another based on a shift to tilting trains.
The latter option would require the franchisee to pay an extra layer of fees to Railtrack to cover the 150 million stg the company estimates a full upgrade will cost, Salmon said.
"We have a firm deal with Railtrack, so franchisees will know what it will cost them in extra charges," he said, adding he saw "a high prospect" that tilting trains would be cheaper.
"If, and I think there's a high prospect of this, bids for tilting trains are cheaper than for conventional, we would simply accept the best bid for the upgrade," Salmon explained.
"If not, then it is for the government to decide," he added.
Part of OPRAF's optimism that new trains will prove to be more economically viable comes from the performance improvements that are expected to accompany a switch to the faster trains.
OPRAF and Railtrack said that tilting trains using upgraded, but still twisting tracks, could cut times significantly from London to Birmingham, Glasgow, Liverpool and Manchester.
